en: Kaccāyana Dhātu Mañjūsā.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
To the Sage who has reached the further shore, crossed over, and gone to the end of grammar (nirutti).
Having paid homage to the Casket of Relics, I shall speak the word of the Buddha in its true sense.
Without resorting to the Agamas of the Sugata or to various grammatical treatises,
I shall here declare the meanings of verbal roots even where they are not explicitly listed in the recited texts.

The vowel *a* following the final consonants of verbal roots (*dhātu*) may optionally become long before the suffixes *si*, *ya*, and *kvaci*; likewise, the vowel preceding the root-final consonant becomes long before the suffixes *yu* and *na*. Furthermore, the word *attha* [is derived from] the root *as* "to be.
*Bhū* is used in the sense of existence (*sattā*); *paca* in cooking (*pāka*); *gamu* and *sappa* in going (*gati*).
*Siloka* is a verbal root meaning accumulation (*saṅghāta*); *saki* occurs in the sense of suspicion (*saṅkā*).
Furthermore, *ku* is used in the sense of taking (*ādāna*), while *ke* and *sadde* are without specific characteristics (*alakkhaṇa*).
*Ku* signifies sound (*sadde*) and that which is contemptible (*kucchite*); *ṭaṅka* means to hold (*dhāraṇe*); *maki* means adornment (*maṇḍane*);
*vaki* refers to crookedness and journeys (*koṭillayātrāsu*); and both *sakka* and *ṭīka* mean gone (*gate*).
*Kak* is used in the sense of longing (*lolattana*), going (*yāta*), and having come (*gata*) here;

(4) *vava* is used for worldly news (*lokanavitti*), the eye’s function (*cakkhavutti*), a tree (*rukkha*), the sky (*khe*), firmness (*thira*), non-injury (*ahiṃsaka*), a moment (*khaṇa*), one's own (*niya*), removal (*apanayi*), clothing (*vatādi*), shaving (*muṇḍi*), initiation (*dikkha*), the armpit (*kakkha*), laughter (*kakhā*), speed (*hasane*), injury (*hiṃsana*), growth (*vuddhi*), and a state of being (*gatī*). (*Hi*) indicates inclusion.

In giving, O Yakṣa, you are considered a consumer; in the miseries of the net, you see both penance and suffering, O you who possess the beauty of the moon. 5. [A] Even in the kiss of a coin, there is learning;
on the stone where lightning arises, there is protection, even in the warding off of guards during the gathering of gleanings.
O monks, whether regarding what is obtained or not obtained, one should abandon the desire for liberation and release amidst those who are obstructed by anger;
one should also speak words that awaken [others].
[Ba] One who guards against *nakha*, *makha*, *rakha*, *naṅkha*, *maṅkha*, *rakkhī*, *ikhīlaṅkhā*, *lakha*, *vakha*, *ikha*, and *iṅkhā*—[this is] *uṅkha*.
*Vaṅkhū*, *ukha*, *gatyam*, *vakhi*, *makhi*, *kakhi*, *kaṅkhe*, *khī*, *khaye*, *ukkha*, *seke*, *khu*,
*khutadhanisu* (is said), *khe* (then), *khāde*,
*supe* (and); *aggo* (however), *gatikoṭille*, *laga*, *saṅge*, *mage*, *āsane*.
*Agī*, *igī*, *rigī*, *ligī*, and *vagī* are verbal roots (*dhātu*) meaning "to go.
*Silāgha* is used in the sense of praising; *jaggha* in laughing; *aggha* in honoring or valuing;
*Sighī* is used in the sense of smelling (*āghrāṇa*); and *laghi* in the senses of drying and going.
*Vaca* means speech; *byattavaca*, eloquent speech; *yāca*, begging; *yācana*, the act of begging;
*ruca*, radiance; *suca*, sorrow; *kuca*, sound; and *vica*, discernment.
*Añca* pertains to worship; *vañca*, going; and *kiñca*, crushing.
*Luñc* is used in the sense of pulling out; *nacca* in dancing; *maca* in shining;
*accā* in going beyond; *cu* in speaking; *saco* in assembly; *paca* in going;
*kaci* and *vacca* in radiance; and *maci* in supporting.
*Puccha* is used in the sense of asking; *muccha*, in the sense of delusion; *lañcha*, in the sense of a mark;
*añchā*, in the sense of stretching; *puñcha*, in the sense of wiping; *uñcha*, in the sense of gleaning;
*taccho*, in the sense of thinning or carving; *piñcha*, in the sense of plucking; and *rāja*, in the sense of splendor.
*Vaj* means to go; *rañj*, to color or dye; *bhañj*, to crush or destroy;
*añj*, to be clear, to go, or beauty; *ej*, to smear; *iñj*, to shake;
*bhaj*, to associate with or serve; *sañj*, to cling; and *iñj*, to shake.
In sacrifice, in divine assemblies, in acts of giving, in bringing about union,
in the threefold endurance, in patience, in giving, and even in the absence of decline;
in embracing one’s own kin, in relinquishing, in creation, in being deluded, and in being submerged.
*Majj* is used for purification; *lajj* for shame; *tajj* for reproaching;
*ajj* for exertion; *sajj* for preparation; *ajjan* for birth; *sajj* for equipment;
*gajj* for thundering; *guj* and *kuj*—both for sound; *khajj* for eating.
*Bhaj* is used in the sense of cooking (*pāka*); *vij* in the sense of fear and trembling (*bhaya-cālana*); *vīj* in the sense of fanning (*vījana*);
*khaj* in the sense of going and deficiency (*gamanavekkale*); *jī* in the sense of conquering (*jaye*); *ju* in the sense of speed (*juve*);
*jhē* in the sense of reflection, exertion, renunciation, and going (*cintā-yujjha-ussagga-gamane*); and *aṭa-paṭa* is a pair [of roots].
*Naṭa* means to dance; *raṭa*, to revile; *vaṭa*, to surround; *vaṭṭa*, to turn;
*vaṇṭa*, in the sense of a share; *kaṭa*, to crush;
*phuṭo*, in the sense of dispersing and so forth; *kaṭa*, to cover and to go.
*Ghuṭ* means sound and striking; *viṭ* means abuse and sending; *bhaṭ* means a servant;
*kuṭ* means breaking and pounding; *luṭ* means rolling;
*jaṭ*, *jhaṭ*, and *piṭ* mean a mass or heap; *ciṭ* means fear; and *ghaṭ* means striking.
*Ghaṭi* means to strike together; *taṭṭa*, to cut; *muṭa*, to crush.
*Paṭha* is used for eloquent speech; *heṭha*, for oppression; *veṭha*, for binding.
The pair *suṭhī* and *kuṭhī* mean to dry up; *pīṭha* means to injure and to support.
*Kaṭha* means drying or cooking; *vaṭha* means stoutness. *Kaṭhi* means to dry;
*ruṭha* and *luṭha* mean injury or destruction; *saṭha* means deceit.
*Haṭha* may mean forceful compulsion; *kaḍi* means breaking; *kaḍiccha* means cutting.
*Maṇḍa* means ornamentation; *caṇḍa*, ferocity; *caṇḍikka*, wrath;
*bhaḍi*, quarreling; *paḍi*, mocking; *liṅga*, deficiency of a mark;
*muḍi*, breaking; *gaḍi*, a part or portion; and *gaḍi* also means a collection.
*Raḍi* and *eraḍi* are used in the sense of harming; *piḍi* in such meanings as crushing or striking together;
*kuḍi* in burning; *paḍi* in falling; *hiḍi* may be used in wandering about;
*karaṇḍa* in the sense of a vessel; and *laḍi* in loathing.
*Vattate* is used in the sense of "measuring" (*meḍa*), "end" (*koṭilla*), "sixth" (*saḍi*), "cluster" (*gumba*), and "stirring" (*thamīraṇa*);
furthermore, *aḍi* is seen in the sense of "egg" (*aṇḍattha*), while *tuḍi* is used for "breaking" (*toḍana*).
*Vaḍḍha* is used for "increasing" (*saṃvaḍḍhana*), *kaḍḍha* for "pulling" (*kaḍḍhaṇa*), and *bhaṇa* for "speaking" (*bhāsana*).
Soṇa occurs in color and the practice of virtues; iṇa and pheṇa both signify debt;
paṇa is used in trade and sacrifice; kaṇa means meeting;
aṇa, raṇa, kaṇa, muṇa, kvaṇa, and kuṇa denote sound.
*Yata* is used in the sense of preparedness; *jūta* in the sense of gambling;
*āta* in the sense of going; *pāta* in the sense of falling; *cita* in the sense of a sign; *saññāṇa* in the sense of a mark;
*kita* in the sense of dwelling; and *vata* in the sense of conduct.
(Bhave): where; *śilāghāyam*: in praise; *matha-mattha*: in churning and agitating;
*nātha*: O Lord; *yācana-santāpa-īśvara-āśiṃsaneṣu*: in begging, distress, sovereignty, and blessings;
*putha* (if used): separate; *puthu*: extensive; *vyatha*: in fear and trembling.
*Gotthu* is used for bamboo, a path, a road, and in the sense of prosperity (*samiddhi*);
*vandā* for salutation, greeting, and praise; *gada* for eloquent speech;
*ninda* for censure and reproach; and *khadi* for leaping forward and so forth.
*Edi* (in this sense) refers to slight movement, radiance, and delight;
*kilidi* refers to lamentation and the moaning directed toward [the deceased];
*idi* (in this sense) refers to supreme sovereignty and the act of binding.
*Bhaga* is used in the sense of service (*sevane*); *bhadra* in the sense of auspicious and noble deeds (*kalyāṇakammani*);
*sīda* in the sense of the ripening of passion (*siṅgārapākesu*); *sadu* in the sense of drying up greenness (*haritasosane*);
*madi* in the sense of strength (*balye*); *muda* and *madā* in the sense of joy (*moda*); *madda* in the sense of contentment (*santose*); and *madda* in the sense of crushing (*maddane*).
*Sandu* means to urinate and so forth; *kanda* means crying out;
*vida* means obtaining; *dada* means giving; *rudi* means shedding tears;
*sado* means fleeing, taking, going, and desponding.
*Hiḷ* means to be pleased (*sukhe*) and *sūd* means to carve (*vilekhaṇe*).

*Sād* is used in the sense of tasting (*assādana*) and so forth; *gad* means eloquent speech (*byattavaca*), and also *nada* means an indistinct sound (*abyattasadda*). *Rad* means to bite (*khāda*) or to eat (*bhakkhaṇa*).
In begging, traveling, and so forth, there may be affection;
(there may be) hunger and thirst, and indeed poverty and misfortune;
but both lead to growth in the two realms, and both—giving and knowing—are found in generosity.
The root *tad* is used in the sense of affliction, such as laziness; *gudh* in the sense of concealment and play;
*atho* in the sense of a firm foundation; *vuṭh* in the sense of growth and increase;
*dhā* in the sense of holding and thought; and *budh* in the sense of awakening.
*Sidh* is used in the sense of going, combat, striking, and piercing;
*rādha* in the sense of harming and attaining; *badha* and *bandha* in the sense of killing and binding;
*sidha* and *sādha* in the sense of accomplishment; *dhe* in the sense of drinking; and *indha* in the sense of radiance.
*Māna* means honor; *vana* means forest-dwelling; *sana* means obtaining;
*ana* means life; *pāna* means drinking; *kana* means a grain; *ditti* means splendor; *gati* means going;
*kantyaṃ* means beauty; *khana* means moment; *khanva* means digging; *avadāraṇe* means splitting. *Gupa* means hiding; *guṇa* means restraint; *tapa* means heat; *tapa* means sovereignty.
The *cupa* is the slow-moving, the *tapuubbege* is the harsh and abusive speech, the *rapa-lapa* is the reproachful word;
the *japa-jappa* is the incoherent chatter, the *tappa* is the act of heating or tormenting (*santappane*),
the *kapi* is the slight movement, the *kiñcicale* is the capability for action, the *kappa* is the power, and the *vepu* is the trembling.
*Tapp* is said to mean "cutting" (*santagata-chede*), *takk* "violence and so forth" (*hiṃsādi*),
*vapa* "sowing seeds" (*bīja-vinikkhepe*), and *dhūpa* "burning" (*santapane*); *capa* means "consolation" (*sāntve*),
*pu* "purifying" (*pavane*), *jhapa* "burning" (*dāhe*), and *supo* "lying down" (*saye*).
*Puppha* means "blooming"; *ramba* and *alamba* mean "hanging down";
*cumba* is considered to mean "kissing" or "contacting the face"; *kamba* is understood as "restraining";
*amba* means "sound" and "taste," while *tāya* means "protection"; and *sabi* means "adornment."
*Gabba* means to deceive; *dappe’bba* means to go; *sabbā’* means to fill;
*gumba* means a cluster; *abbagumbana* means to be crowded; *cabba* means to eat;
*ubba* means to hold; *labha* means gain; *lābhe* means obtaining; *jambha* means the bending of limbs; *subha* means beauty.
*Bhī* is used in the sense of fear; *rabha* in the sense of impetuosity (*rābhasya*) and undertaking (*ārambha*);
*khubha* in the sense of agitation; *thambha* and *khambha* in the sense of obstruction; *gabbha* in the sense of arrogance (*pāgabbhiya*) and killing;
*sumbha* in the sense of crushing (*saṃsumbhana*); *sambha* in the sense of trust (*vissāsa*); and *yabha* in the sense of sexual intercourse (*methuna*).
The root *dubh* is used in the sense of seeking to injure; *dabbha* in the sense of binding with grass;
*udrabh* in the sense of lifting up; *kamū* in the sense of stepping forward;
*khamū* in the sense of enduring; *bhamu* in the sense of instability; and *vamu* in the sense of vomiting and so forth.
*Kila* and *klamū* are used for illness; *ramu* for play (*kīḷā*).
*Dama* is used for self-control (*dame*), *nama* for bowing (*name*), and likewise *sama* for fatigue (*parissame*).
*Yamu* is used for cessation (*uparame*) and destruction (*nāse*); *ama* for going (*yāte*), and *mu* for binding (*bandhane*).
*Dhamo* and *pumō* mean "blowing"; *dhamana* means "adorned with doubt.
*Dhuma* and *thīma* mean "aggregation"; *tama* means "consolation" and "destruction.
*Ayo*, *vayo*, *paya*, *mayo*, and *nayo* refer to "motion" (*rayagati*).
For *daya* is found in giving, going, and protection; in harming and so forth, it is mixed (*yu*).
In movement, honoring, and by that [means], in the growth of merit within the continuum;
and furthermore, in envy, the manifestation of hatred, and in lying down (*sāya*), it is *sā*.
*Tara* is in the sense of crossing over; *thara* in the sense of spreading out; *bhara* in the sense of supporting; *phara* in the sense of pervading;
*sara* in the senses of motion, thought, injury, and sound; *phura* in the sense of trembling and so forth; *hara* in the sense of taking away;
*ri* in the sense of continuous flow and motion; *ru* in the sense of sound; *khura* in the sense of cutting; and *dhara* in the sense of holding.
*Jara* means aging; *jīraṇa*, decay; *marapāṇacāge*, the giving up of life; *khara*, harshness; *sekanāse*, destruction by sprinkling; *ghara*, a house; *sevanamhi*, in the sense of resorting to.
*Garo* means swallowing; *nigareṇa*, by way of vomiting; *seke*, in sprinkling; *dara*, fear; *ḍāhe*, burning;
*vidāraṇe*, tearing apart. *Cara* means movement and eating; *vara* means restraint and so forth.
Caracchede, Aranāse, Gate, Pūra, Pūraṇe, Kura, Kose,
Nara, Naye, Jāgara, Supinakkhaye; Pīlu, Palū,
Sala, Hulā, Gatya, Atthā, Cala, Kampane.
*Khala* is used in the sense of moving; *phulla* in the sense of blooming;
*jala* in the sense of giving light; *phala* in the sense of fruition; *dala* in the sense of shining and splitting;
*duggati* in the sense of a miserable state; *nīla* in the sense of the color blue; and *mīla* in the sense of closing.
*Silā* means a stake, binding, swallowing, eating, a bank, an obstruction, a spear, pain, and strength;
*tala* and *mūla* mean a foundation; *vala* and *valla* mean warding off.
*Palla* occurs in the senses of "low," "going," "impurity," and "wrestling";
*khila* in "barrenness" and "hardness"; the pair *kala* and *kalā* in "mud" and "a small part";
*vela* in "movement" and "tide"; *kalla* in "ready" and "sound"; and *alī* in "binding."
In the minor shaking, the major tossing, and the minor crushing;
(it) proceeds in the cases of purity, protection, and reaching;
in the shaking, moving, clothing, carrying, and swaying, and so forth.
*Ava* is used in the sense of protection (*rakkhaṇa*), *jīva* in the sense of sustaining life (*pāṇadhāraṇa*), and *plava* in the sense of going (*gata*).
*Kaṇḍuva* is used in the sense of scratching (*kaṇḍuvana*), *saraṇa* in the sense of refuge (*saraṇa*), and *dava* in the sense of cutting (*chedana*).
*Dava* is used in the sense of forest fire (*davane*), *devu* in the sense of playing (*devane*), and *sevu* in the sense of serving (*sevane*).
*Dhāva* is taught in the sense of going (*gamanavuddhi*); *dhovu* is used for washing (*dhovane*);
*ve* and *vī* are both used for weaving threads (*tantusantāna*); *veu* may be used for restraining (*saṃvaraṇa*);
*hve* is used for calling (*avhāna*); *keva* is used for sprinkling (*seka*); and *dhuva* is used for maintenance (*yātrā*) and firmness (*thira*).
*Asa* means eating; *ghasa* means in the act of eating; *isa* means in distress; *isu* means desire;
*sasū* means by means of harming living beings; *masa* means in the sense of touching; *musa* means in falsehood; *kusa* means in abuse;
*dusa* means in displeasure; *tusa* means in contentment; *pusa* means in nourishment.
*Rus* means to come; *hiṃs* means to injure; *mas* means to be stingy; *usu* means burning; *has* means laughing;
*ghus* means sound; *tas* means fear; *tras* means to tremble with fear;
*las* means beauty; *ras* means taste; and *bhas* means to reduce to ashes.
*Gavesa* means seeking; *maggaṇe*, searching; *nāsane*, destroying; *disa*, looking at the directions; *sāsā*, instruction; *anuṣṭhiyaṃ*, following;
*haṃsa*, joy; *pitiyaṃ*, delight; *pāsa*, binding with a snare; *bandhane*, fettering; *saṃsa*, praise;
*pasaṃsane*, extolling; *issa*, envy; *issāyaṃ*, jealousy; *kassa*, who?; *kassane*, asking.
*Dhaṃsa* is in the sense of falling away; *siṃsa* in the sense of desire; *ghaṃsa* in the sense of rubbing;
*saṃsa* and *daṃsā* in the sense of biting; *bhāsa* in the sense of speech and radiance;
*bhusa* may be used in the sense of ornamenting; and *āsū* in the sense of entering.
*Vasa* is used in the senses of dwelling, rain, sprinkling, and sound;
*kisa* in the sense of being emaciated; *sāṇa* in the sense of hemp; *kasa* in the sense of going and harming or scratching;
*disā* in the sense of direction, wicked people, and so forth; and *kāsa* in the sense of brilliance and attachment.
The roots *khasa* and *jhasa* mean "to injure"; *misa*, "to meet";
*su* [is used] in the senses of injury, a group, connection, journey, and so forth;
*su* [is used] in the sense of sound, and *si* in the senses of procreation and service (*sevane*).
*Maha* means worthy of great worship (*arahapūjā*); *guha* means concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*); *liha* means enjoyment (*assāda*); *raha* means in generosity (*cāga*);
*muha* means infatuation (*mucchā*); *maha* means a being (*sattā*); *bahu* means in number (*saṃkhyāna*); *saha* means patience (*khama*);
*daha* means burning to ashes (*bhasmikaraṇa*); and *patiṭṭhāyaṃ* means in a foundation.
*Ūha* is used in the sense of producing growth and reflection; *vaha* in carrying;
*duha* in filling and destroying; *diha* is considered to mean accumulation;
*garaha* in censuring; *īha* in exertion; and *miha* in service.
*Gāha* is used in the sense of agitating; *brūha*, *baha*, and *braha* in the sense of growth;
*vhe* in the sense of sound; *hasa* in the sense of laughing; *hā* in the sense of giving up; *luḷa* in the sense of churning;
*laḷa* in the sense of play, sport, and dalliance (these are [roots] with the vowel increment *e*).

The *tuda*-group roots are those that do not undergo vowel strengthening (*avuddhi*): *tuda* in the sense of "afflicting," *nuda* in the sense of "pushing away," *likha* in the sense of "scratching," *kuca* in the sense of "contracting," *rica* in the sense of "leaving," and *khaca* in the sense of "binding."
The root *vas* is used in the sense of sound and assembly; *vijī* in the sense of fear and movement;
*bhuja* in the sense of crookedness; *valañja* in the sense of using;
*bhaja* in the sense of service and separation; and *ruja* in the sense of disease and wandering.
In the cutting of wood, crookedness, houses, recitation (*svādhyāya*),
and so forth; again, in beautiful deeds, conduct, turning, begging,
cooking separately, putrefaction, and also in affliction (*saṃkleśana*).
The two roots *dhū* signify "to spread" in the sense of expansion (*vitthāre*) and "to know" (*vida-jānane*);
*had* signifies "excretion" (*uccāra-ussagge*) and "thought" (*cintāyaṃ*); *mid* signifies "injury" (*hiṃsane*);
*nandh* signifies "binding" (*vinandhane*); and *thīna* further signifies "solidification" (*saṅghāta-vācino*).
*Kapa* is used in the sense of covering (*acchādane*), *vappa* in the sense of warding off (*vāraṇe*), and *khipa* in the sense of throwing (*peraṇe*);
*Supa* is used in the sense of lying down (*saye*), *chupa* in the sense of touching (*phasse*);
*Capa* is used in the sense of consoling (*sāntvane*), *nabha* (the root) in the sense of harming (*vihiṃsāyaṃ*), and *rumbha* in the sense of pressing (*uppīḷanādisu*).
Sumbha in crushing, jambha in devouring, jubha in ejecting,
ṭhubha in spitting out, camu in eating, chamu in contempt,
jhamu in burning, chamu in eating, and irīya in moving about (as well as).
*Kir* (as a root) is used in the sense of scattering;
*gir* in swallowing and so forth; *phur* in trembling and the like; *kur* in sound and taking;
*khur* in cutting and scratching; and *ghur* in the terrible and swallowing.
*Tila* means oil; *cila* means dwelling; *hila* means emotion; *silu* means cleaning; *bila* means a hole or fissure; *thūla* means a heap;
*kusacchedana* means cutting grass; *pūraṇa* means filling;
*visappavese* means the spreading of poison; *pharaṇe* means pervading; and it is used in such senses as "sending out in all directions."
*Phu* is used for *phassati*, *mu* for *musāti*, *tha* for *theyyāya*, and *thu* for *appikirayāya*;
*gu* is used for *mokkhe* and *gu* for *parivattane* (and so on for *tudādayo*); *hū* represents the roots beginning with *bhū* when the *vikaraṇa* suffixes have been elided (*luttavikaraṇā*).
*Hū-bhū* [are used] in the sense of existence (*sattā*) and in the sense of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and destiny (*gati*);
*khā-khyā* [are used] in the sense of the two types of explanation (*pakathana*); *ji* [is used] in the sense of victory (*jaya*) and knowledge/awakening (*ñāṇavabodhana*);
*sī-ḷī* [are used] in the sense of moving through the air (*vehāsagamana*); *ṭhā* [is used] in the sense of cessation from movement (*gatīvinivutti*).
*Ū* is used for evil, *mū* for knowledge, and *ha* for killing or injury;
*pā* is used for protection, *pā* for drinking, *brū* for articulate speech,
*bhā* for splendor, and *mā* for measure (as well as that which may be reached).
The root *du* is used in the senses of seizing (*ādāna*) or moving (*gatigandhana*);
*as* is known as the element for existence (*bhū*), and *si* is used in the sense of lying down (*śaye*).
Roots such as *juhoty-ādi* take six case-endings (*sad-vibhakti*) and undergo elision of their *vikaraṇa* suffixes.
The root *hū* occurs in the senses of giving (*dāna*), taking (*ādāna*), and offering oblations (*havyadāna*);

*hā* in the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*); *kamu* in the sense of wandering about (*yātrā*); *dā* in the sense of giving (*dāna*); and *dhā* in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇa*). The roots beginning with *bhū* that do not take verbal suffixes (*avikaraṇa*) are completed.
The roots beginning with *rudh* are: *rudh* (to obstruct), *muc* (to release), *ric* (to empty),
*sic* (to sprinkle), *yuj* (to join), and *bhuj* (to protect and to eat).
*Kṛt* means cutting; *chid* means splitting in two; *bhid* means cleaving or rending;
*vid* means obtaining; *lup* means cutting off or destruction;
*lip* means smearing; *piṣ* means crushing; *his* means injury—these belong to the *rudhādi* class.
The *divādi* roots:
*divu* means play, desire to conquer, commerce, and splendor;
*sivu* means the continuity of threads; *khī* means destruction; *khā* means manifestation.
*Kā* in the sense of sound (*sadde*); *ghā* in the sense of smell (*gandhe*); *upādāne* (in the sense of clinging); *ruca* and *rocane* (in the sense of liking);
*kaca* in the sense of shining (*dittim*); *muca* and *moce* (in the sense of releasing);

*vica* in the sense of discerning (*vivecane*); *rañja* in the sense of passion (*rāge*); *sañja* in the sense of attachment (*saṅge*); *khalane* (in the sense of stumbling); *majja* in the sense of purification (*suddhiyaṃ*).
*Yu* is in the sense of concentration; *lu* is in destruction; *jha* is in reflection; *tā* is in protection;
*chi* is in cutting into two; *da* is in softening; *mi* is in affection; *madu* is in intoxication;
*umma* is in madness; *khida* is in dejection; *bhidā* is in splitting apart.
The root *sid* is used in the sense of ripening, falling away, and knowing; *vid* in the sense of reflecting;
*dī* in the sense of destruction and sleeping; *dā* in the sense of giving and cutting;
and *yudh* in the sense of battle and understanding the Buddhas and so forth.
*Kudha* is used in the sense of anger (*kope*); *sudha* in the sense of sorrow (*soce*); and *rādha* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsāya*).
*Siddhiyaṃ* [is used] in the sense of perfection and growth (*saṃsiddhi-vuddhīsu*) in this world; likewise, *sidha* and *sādha* are used in the sense of perfection (*siddhiyaṃ*).
*Vidha* is used in the sense of piercing (*vedhe*); *gidha* in the sense of greed (*gedhe*); and *rudhi* in the sense of obstruction and so forth (*āvaraṇādisu*).
*Man* is used in the senses of mind, knowledge, birth, production, killing, and going;
*sinā* means to wash and to grieve; *kup* means anger; *tap* means heat and torment;
*lup* means cutting off; *rup* means destruction; *dip* means to illuminate and light.
*Dapa* is pride; *hāsa* is laughter; *labha* is gain; *lābha* is greed for profit; *gedha* is covetousness; *khubho* is agitation; *cale* is wavering;
*samū’pasama* is tranquility; *kheda* is weariness; *hara* is shamelessness; *hirī* is modesty; *lajjane* is bashfulness; *milā* is withered;
*gattavīnāma* is emaciation of the limbs; *gilā* is illness; and *hāsakkhaye* is the cessation of laughter.
*Lī* is used in the senses of adhesion (*silese*), liquefaction (*dravīkāre*), and movement (*gatī*) among bonds (*bandhanesu*);
*lisi* and *lese* mean satisfaction (*tose*); *silisā* refers to embracing (*aliṅganādi*) and so forth;
*kilisa* and *kalisa* mean affliction (*apatāpe*); and *tasa* means thirst (*pipāsane*).
*Rusa* occurs in the sense of rising up and in the sense of enmity (*appīti*);
[the root] *asu* occurs in the sense of bestowing glory (*yasuppāyana*) and also in the sense of wasting away (*khepana*);
*susa* in the sense of drying up (*sosana*), *bhasa* in the sense of falling down (*adhopāta*), and *nasa* in the sense of non-perception (*adassana*).

116. *Sā* is used in the sense of enjoyment (*assāde*), in the end (*avasāne*), and also in the sense of attenuation (*tanūkaraṇe*). *Hā* is used in the sense of giving up (*cāge*), in mental distress (*muhecitte*), and not in the sense of binding the virtuous (*na ha sajjana-bandhane*). *Naha* is used in the sense of sorrow (*soce*), desire (*pihicchāyaṃ*), and joy accompanied by affection (*sineha-sineha-pītiyaṃ*). 117.
*Su* is used in the sense of hearing (*savaṇe*), *saka* in the sense of power (*sattimhi*), *khī* in the sense of destruction (*khayamhi*), and *gi* in the sense of sound (*saddane*).
The root *apa-sambhū* is used in the senses of attaining, going, and restraint;
*kiyā-* and others [beginning with *kī*] in exchange; *ci* in accumulation; *ji* in victory; and *ñā* in understanding.
*Tha* is used in the sense of praising (*abhitthave*), shaking (*kampane*), and blowing (*pavane*).
*Dhu* is used in the sense of burning (*tappaṇe*), measuring (*māne*), throwing (*khipakkhepe*), and harming (*hiṃsane*).
*Mi* is used in the sense of measuring (*māne*) and binding (*bandhe*). *Lu* is used in the sense of cutting off (*pacchede*), and *si* is used in the sense of binding (*bandhane*).
Asa is used in the sense of eating; gaha in the sense of grasping; kiyā and others;
tanā and others in the sense of expansion; saka in the sense of power; du in the sense of affliction; and sanu in the sense of giving.
In the sense of "going" (*yā*), [the root] *manu* occurs; in the sense of "attaining" (*pāpuṇana*), [the root] *apa*; in the sense of "doing" (*karaṇa*), [the root] *kara*;
in the sense of "binding" (*bandha*), [the roots] *si*, *bandhi*, and so on; and in the sense of "flowing forth" (*abhissavana*), [the roots] *tanu* and others.
Those beginning with *cur* are always used in the sense of "stealing" (*ṇeyanta*).
*Thi* occurs in the sense of curing, the world, a realm, seeing, a drop, and a characteristic;
*thaka* may mean to stop or to strike; *taka* means reasoning or reflecting;
*lak* occurs in the sense of a characteristic, seeing, or a mark; and *makkha* means to smear.
In eating food, in liberation, in release, and in pleasure and pain;
in the movement of the body, in the movement of the mind, and so forth; in the path and the seeking of the path;
and furthermore, in the fivefold expansion, in defilement, in deception, and in apprehension.
*Vac* is used in the sense of reciting (*ajjhāyana*), *acc* in the sense of honoring (*pūjā*), *vac* in the sense of speaking (*bhāsana*);
*rac* in the sense of preparing (*paṭiyatana*), *suc* in the sense of backbiting (*pesuñña*), and *ruc* in the sense of shining (*rocana*);
*muc* in the sense of releasing (*ppamocana*), *loc* in the sense of seeing (*dassana*), and *kac* in the sense of radiance (*ditti*).
*Sajjā* means "prepared" today; *tajja* means "reproaching"; *vajja* means "faulty";
*yuja* means "in restraint"; *pūja* means "in worship"; *tija* means "sharpening";
*paja* means "obstructing the path"; and *bhaja* means "dividing."
*Bhāja* means to divide; *sabhāja*, to show affection;
*ghaṭa*, to join together; *ghaṭṭa*, to move and so forth;
*kuṭa* and *koṭṭa*, both meaning to cut; and *kuṭa*, to strike and so forth.
*Naṭa* means to dance; *caṭa*, to split open; *vaṇṭa*, to divide;
*tuvaṭṭa*, to lie on one's back; *ghaṭo*, in the sense of dispersing;
*guṇṭha*, to cover; *heṭha*, in the sense of oppression; *veṭha*, to wrap.
*Guḍi* means to sit; *kaḍi*, *khaḍi*, and *bhedane* mean to break;
*maḍi* means to adorn; *paṇḍa* and *bhaṇḍa* mean to revile; *daḍi* is defined as a command;
*taḍi* means to strike; *piṇḍa* means to collect; and *chaḍḍa* means to abandon.
*Vaṇṇa* means to praise or describe; *cuṇṇa*, to grind into powder; *āṇa*, to command or send;
*gaṇa*, to count or calculate; *kaṇṇa*, to hear; *cinta*, to think or reflect;
*santa*, to contract or shrink; *manta*, to speak secretly or to know.
The root *cita* is used in the sense of volition (*saṃcetanā*) and so forth; *kitta* in the sense of praising (*saṃsaddana*);
*yata* in the sense of leading away (*nīyyātana*), binding (*gantha*), composition (*sandabbha*), and requesting (*atthayācana*);
*katha* in the sense of a continuous sequence of speech (*vākyappabandha*); *vida* in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*); and *nuda* in the sense of urging (*cuda*).
*Chadā* means "invitation" (*apavāraṇa*), "vomiting" (*vamana*), "will" (*chanda*), and "desire" (*icchā*).
*Vadī* is used in the sense of "salutation" (*abhivāda*) and "praise" (*thoma*); *bhadī* refers to "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*) deeds.
*Hiḷāda* (but *hiḷā*) means "happiness" (*sukha*); *gandha* means "indication" (*sūcana*); *vidha* means "shaking" (*kampana*).
*Randha* is used in the sense of cooking (*pāka*), as well as in pride (*māna*), honor (*pūjā*), and praise (*thuṭi*);
*thana* in the sense of a place (*ṭhāna*) and the sound of gods (*devasadda*); *ūna* in the sense of deficiency (*parihāni*) and theft (*thena*);
*dhana* in the sense of wealth (*dhana*); and *ñapa* in the sense of pleasing (*tosa*), sharpening (*nisāna*), killing (*māraṇa*), and so forth.
*Lapa* means speaking; *jhapa*, burning; *rupa*, planting and so forth;
*pī*, distressing; *kappa*, possibility; *vitakka*, reflection; *labhi*, deceiving; (*atho*), moreover;
*vahi*, reproaching; *samu*, consolation; and *dassana*, showing.
*Kamu* is used in the sense of desire, beauty, praise, and commendation;
*timu* in the sense of wetness, suspicion, and being afflicted by disease and so forth;
*saṃgāma* in the sense of battle and war; and *īra* in the sense of speech and trembling.
*Vara* is used in the sense of choice or a boon; *āvaraṇi* in the sense of concealment; *icchā* in the sense of desire; *yācā* in the sense of begging;
*dhara* and *dhāraṇa* in the sense of holding or supporting; *tīra* in the sense of completion of an action; *pāra* in the sense of capability and so forth; *tula* in the sense of measuring;
*khala* in the sense of threshing floor or chaff; *sova* in the sense of accumulation; and *pāla* in the sense of protection.
*Kala* is used in the sense of calculation and so forth; *mīla* in closing the eyes;
*sīla* in upholding virtue; *mūla* in growing; *lala* in desiring;
*dula* in lifting up; *pūla* in greatness and accumulation.
*Ghusa* means sound; *pisa* and *pesa* mean ornamenting with grass;
*rusa* means harshness; *khuṃsa* means abuse; *pusa* means nourishing;
*disa* means utterance and so forth; *vasa* means covering.
*Ra* is used for taste, enjoyment, sound, affection, and furthermore, for lead and distinction;
*si* is for binding, mixing, mingling, and it may be used for deception;
*raha* is for abandonment and going, while *ma* is prescribed for honor.
*Pihi* occurs in the sense of desire; *vīḷa* in the sense of shame; *eḷa* in the sense of breaking;
*hīḷa* in the sense of reproaching; *pīḷa* in the sense of oppression; *taḷa* in the sense of striking;
and *laḷa* in the sense of indulgence. These belong to the *mecurādi* group.
The seven groups [of verbal roots] are complete:
the *bhū*-class, the *rudh*-class, the *div*-class, the *svādi*-class,
the *kryādi*-class, the *tan*-class, and the *curādi*-class— thus they are sevenfold here.
The meaning of many roots has been declared by me for the sake of explaining the various words;
for roots indeed possess multiple meanings, which must be understood through their application.
For the benefit of those of dull intellect, I have explained them clearly, in the order of their phonemes, and concisely.
This *Dhātumañjūsā* was composed by the wise Sīlavaṃsa;
Sīlavaṃsa was a royal swan in the lotus pond of the True Dhamma,
who established the endurance of the Dhamma.
This Yatissara, a resident of the dwelling known as Yakkhaddila, has composed this;
thus ends the *Kaccāyana-dhātumañjūsā*.
The supplementary rules taught by the Teacher:
A single [vowel] is the substitute for many [consonants], with *r* as the final element;
for both [types of suffixes], the final vowels are called "limbs" (*aṅga*) and "subsequent elements" (*anubandha*) of verbal roots, respectively.
The consonants of a base (dhātu) are preceded by the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), with the final letter being the same as the last [consonant] of the preceding word;
those beginning with *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, etc., are marked by an *anubandha*.
All other *anubandhas* serve the purpose of indicating pronunciation (*uccāraṇa*).
Verbal roots yield various results depending on the difference in their application; even when they function as nouns,
they are employed in certain instances according to their specific role in an action,
provided there is no contradiction with other intervening factors.
In certain instances, when a case-ending follows a dvanda compound, a single substitute is prescribed for that ending;
likewise, even a word [ending in a vowel] undergoes the state of *guṇa* and so forth when it occurs in the sense of *tad-kriyā* (that action).
